title: Motion for Leave to File Supplemental Comments and Supplemental Comments of Buckeye Power, Inc. on the 09/10/2026 filing by Dayton Power and Light Company under ER26-3752.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

      The Dayton Power and Light Company                      Docket No. ER26-3752-000


        MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS AND
          SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS OF BUCKEYE POWER, INC.

           Pursuant to Rule 212 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC”

or “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 Buckeye Power, Inc. (“Buckeye”) 2

respectfully submits these supplemental comments on the September 10, 2026 filing 3 by

the Dayton Power and Light Company (“AES Ohio”) in the above-captioned proceeding.

The filing contains a Construction Service Agreement (“CSA”), with a form electric

distribution service agreement (“ESA”) attached as Exhibit E, between AES Ohio and a

data center load (“Customer”).

           On October 1, 2026, Buckeye filed comments on the public version of the AES

Ohio Filing and filed a motion requesting that the Commission direct AES Ohio to

provide the unredacted version of the Filing. 4 AES Ohio provided the unredacted Filing

to Buckeye on October 14, 2026, 5 and Buckeye and AES Ohio filed a Joint Answer on

October 15, 2026 mutually agreeing to allow Buckeye to file supplemental comments on

  Motion to Compel Production of Non-Public Version of the Filing, Request for Extended Comment
Period, and Limited Comments of Buckeye Power Inc. (Oct. 1, 2026), eLibrary No. 20261001-5273
(“Buckeye’s Comments”).
5
 Joint Answer to Motion for Leave to Answer Out of Time of Buckeye Power, Inc. and The Dayton Power
and Light Company at 1 (Oct. 15, 2026), eLibrary No. 20261015-5109 (“Joint Answer”).
 or before October 22, 2026 to resolve Buckeye’s October 1, 2026 Motion to Compel. 6 As

contemplated in the Joint Answer, Buckeye is filing these Supplemental Comments to

address additional concerns based on review of the complete filing.

              As stated in Buckeye’s Comments, Buckeye supports AES Ohio’s stated

commitment to protect all transmission customers of AES Ohio from increased

transmission costs associated with transmission investments to serve new, large data

center load. AES Ohio’s parent company, AES Corp, along with numerous data center

owners and developers have signed the White House’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, and

Buckeye commends AES Ohio’s statements in the Filing consistent with that

commitment. 7 Buckeye believes these commitments to ensure “higher of” pricing and

prevent cost shifting to other customers are appropriate for data centers, whose load

characteristics and long-term demand profile differ significantly from traditional

manufacturing facilities that support American industry, create substantial and lasting

jobs, and have an established history of sustained energy use. The targeted application of

these customer protections to new data center loads is further demonstrated by AES

Ohio’s retail tariff proposal in a recent stipulation submitted to the Public Utilities

Commission of Ohio (“PUCO”), which applies exclusively to data center load. 8

              Review of the full Filing, however, raises concerns about whether other

transmission customers will actually be protected in practice:

          •   First, AES Ohio states that the CSA requires the data center Customer to take a
              minimum level of service “that will produce revenues that equal or exceed the

 Ratepayer Protection Pledge, The White House, https://www.whitehouse.gov/ratepayer-protection-
pledge/ (last visited Oct. 21, 2026).

PUCO review in PUCO Docket No. 25-0958-EL-AIR et al.

             costs of the Network Upgrades.” 9 The Network Upgrades specified in the CSA
            are significant, and Buckeye’s preliminary analysis indicates that the Customer’s
            payments may not cover the Network Upgrade costs even if the data center
            Customer’s load shows up at the full 100% expected amount, resulting in the
            transmission rate increasing for all other customers. Given the serious potential
            for cost shifting presented in this CSA, the Commission should confirm that the
            “future AES Ohio rate case” 10 to address the rate treatment of the facilities listed
            in the CSA must be filed under Federal Power Act (“FPA”) section 205, 16
            U.S.C. § 824d. Doing so will ensure that this future proceeding follows the full
            statutory provisions for public utility rate changes.

       •    Second, AES Ohio commits to credit any exit fee payments it receives pursuant to
            the CSA (or attached ESA) to its Attachment H-15 formula rate to avoid double
            recovery of Network Upgrade costs. 11 But AES Ohio fails to include in this
            commitment any formula rate credits for payments it receives for (1) Minimum
            Load charges collected in section 5.d of the ESA, or (2) deferral costs recovered
            in section 3 of the CSA. These provisions must also be included in AES Ohio’s
            commitment to avoid double counting, otherwise other wholesale transmission
            customers will not be protected against transmission cost shifting—which AES
            Ohio states is its intent.

            Even if this CSA is reviewed subject to the Mobile Sierra public interest standard,

the Commission is statutorily mandated to ensure that this bilateral agreement between

AES Ohio and a large data center Customer does not present a risk of serious harm to the

public interest. 12 As Chairman Swett and Commissioner LaCerte have explained, “the

Mobile-Sierra presumption is not a straw man behind which the Commission hides to

evade its statutory duty of ensuring that the American consumer pays just and reasonable




9
  Transmittal Letter at 8-9. In order to ensure that “higher of” pricing is implemented, and transmission
rates are not raised for other customers, it is necessary that the Customer’s payments cover not just the
Network Upgrade costs, but also the associated return, depreciation, taxes, and other costs that are paid by
transmission customers through AES Ohio’s transmission formula rates through the term of service. Any
references in these Supplemental Comments to AES Ohio’s commitment to ensure the Customer covers the
Network Upgrade costs assumes the Customer will cover the incremental annual revenue requirement
associated those Network Upgrades over the term of service to ensure the transmission costs of other
customers are not increased.

     Morgan Stanley Cap. Grp. Inc. v. Pub. Util. Dist. No. 1 of Snohomish Cnty., 554 U.S. 527, 530 (2008).



                                                     -3-
 rates.” 13

         The Commission should require AES Ohio to: (1) confirm that the “future AES

Ohio rate case” proceeding on the rate treatment for the facilities contemplated in the

CSA will be filed pursuant to FPA section 205 in order to ensure other transmission

customers are not bearing the costs of Network Upgrades made to serve data centers; and

(2) include the Minimum Load charges and deferral costs consistent with its commitment

to protect against double recovery in footnote 19, or explain why Minimum Load charges

and deferral costs are excluded from this commitment.

I.       MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS

         As noted above, AES Ohio’s and Buckeye’s Joint Answer agrees that allowing

Buckeye to file supplemental comments on or before October 22, 2026 would resolve

Buckeye’s October 1, 2026 Motion to Compel. Buckeye is submitting these

Supplemental Comments by that date. Additional good cause exists for granting this

Motion for Leave to File Supplemental Comments. Buckeye was not provided an

unredacted version of the CSA at issue in this proceeding until after the original comment

deadline had passed, despite submitting an executed Nondisclosure Certificate to AES

Ohio well in advance of that deadline. After receiving the unredacted version, Buckeye

engaged in expedited review of the full Filing in order to file this Motion and its

Supplemental Comments within six business days. Accepting these Supplemental




13

concurring) (citing 16 U.S.C. § 824d(a)). “If the circumstances demonstrate serious harm to the public
interest, and especially harm to third parties such as ultimate ratepayers, the Commission has a statutory
responsibility to take action.” Id. (citing NRG Power Mktg., LLC v. Me. Pub. Util. Comm’n, 558 U.S. 165,
174 (2010)).

 Comments will aid in the Commission’s understanding of the issues raised in AES

Ohio’s Filing.

II.         SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS

            A. The Commission should require that the future filing seeking rolled in
               rate treatment is filed pursuant to Federal Power Act section 205.

            AES Ohio represents in its transmittal letter that the CSA contemplates AES Ohio

seeking rolled-in rate treatment for the costs of Network Upgrades “based on the

expectation that revenues paid by Customer pursuant to the ESA will more than offset the

cost of service for such upgrades during the term.” 14 It goes on to state that: 15

                    Customer in the CSA effectively has committed to take a
                    minimum level of transmission service that will produce
                    revenues that equal or exceed the costs of the Network
                    Upgrades necessary to safely and reliably serve Customer,
                    thereby protecting AES Ohio and its other transmission
                    customers from potential adverse cost shifts associated with
                    rolled in pricing for the new service.

            Buckeye supports AES Ohio’s stated commitment, consistent with the data center

Ratepayer Protection Pledge, to require sufficient payments by the data center Customer

so that other transmission customers are protected against increased transmission prices.

            AES Ohio claims that it structured the CSA to be “consistent with Commission’s

‘higher of’ transmission pricing policies which allow transmission providers to charge

rolled-in, embedded cost rates, rather than incremental rates, when the embedded cost

rate will generate revenues that exceed the incremental costs of providing service.” 16 As

 AES Ohio notes, “higher of” pricing is intended to ensure that: 17

                      When a transmission provider agrees to rolled-in pricing for
                      new transmission service, the customer signs a transmission
                      service agreement committing to take long-term service that
                      will produce revenues that exceed the incremental costs to
                      provide transmission service. In this manner, the
                      transmission provider and its other transmission customers
                      are protected from cost shifts that could arise from providing
                      the new transmission service.

But if rolling in the costs of new transmission facilities does not result in payments that

equal or exceed the incremental costs to provide transmission service, then other

customers are not protected against transmission rate increases. In its preliminary review

of the details of the CSA, Buckeye is unable to verify that the Customer’s payments will

protect AES Ohio’s other customers, including Buckeye and its members, from increased

transmission rates.

            AES Ohio states that the “rate treatment of such proceeds should be appropriately

addressed in a future AES Ohio rate case, not this proceeding.” 18 And Buckeye

recognizes that in response to CSAs previously filed by AES Ohio, the Commission has

held that “the appropriate allocation of Network Upgrade costs is not before the

Commission in this proceeding and will be determined in further proceedings.” 19 Given

the serious potential for cost shifting here, and AES Ohio’s commitment pursuant to the

Ratepayer Protection Pledge to ensure data centers pay for their costs and do not raise

costs for other customers, the Commission should direct AES Ohio to provide more

information on that future proceeding to ensure that these issues can be fully and properly


17
  Id. (emphasis added) (footnote omitted) (citing Pub. Serv. Co. of N.M., 177 FERC ¶ 61,094, P 19
(2021)).
18
     Id. at 9 n.19.
19
     Dayton Power & Light Co., 195 FERC ¶ 61,239, P 15 (2026).



                                                  -6-
 addressed in that proceeding.

       The appropriate vehicle for this future “rate case” is an AES Ohio filing pursuant

to FPA section 205, which provides an opportunity for Commission review and

participation by customers such as Buckeye. Consistent with the Federal Power Act, AES

Ohio should bear the burden of showing that its proposed rate treatment is just,

reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory.

       It is important to clarify that the future “rate case” will be a section 205 filing

because merely including these costs in transmission rates through a formula rate annual

update would not be consistent with AES Ohio’s intention to seek rolled-in rate treatment

in a future rate case. Annual updates are informational filings that seek to implement

formula rates on file with the Commission, and AES Ohio has not reformed its formula or

protocols to transparently and specifically address these important issues of large load-

driven costs. As such, the annual update process may not provide the information

necessary for stakeholders and the Commission to determine whether the “higher of”

pricing commitment has been met, nor be an appropriate opportunity to impose

incremental pricing if necessary to ensure other customers’ rates are not increased.

       The Commission should therefore require AES Ohio to confirm that the “future

AES Ohio rate case” proceeding to address the rate treatment of the facilities under the

CSA will be filed pursuant to section 205.

       B. AES Ohio should provide additional clarifications in footnote 19 to
          ensure all customers are protected from cost shifting.

       AES Ohio states that the goal of the CSA is “to ensure that AES Ohio could

reliably transmit and distribute energy to the Data Center to meet its expected load while

protecting its other customers from potential cost increases if the Data Center fails to take



                                             -7-
 service as expected.” 20 To effectuate this goal, as in prior filings of similar CSAs, AES

Ohio has committed that: 21

                      In order to avoid the potential for double recovery of
                      Network Upgrade costs, AES Ohio agrees that, if the
                      Network Upgrade costs are rolled into its transmission rates
                      under Attachment H-15 of the PJM OATT and if Customer
                      subsequently makes a payment to AES Ohio of the Network
                      Upgrade costs incurred under CSA Section 7 and 14 or
                      Exhibit E – ESA Section 2.c.ii of the CSA, AES Ohio will
                      appropriately reflect Customer’s payment in its transmission
                      cost of service under Attachment H-15. However, rate
                      treatment of such proceeds should be appropriately
                      addressed in a future AES Ohio rate case, not this
                      proceeding.

            While Buckeye has supported similar commitments by AES Ohio with respect to

prior CSAs, 22 the Commission should direct AES Ohio to clarify the scope of the

commitment here. AES Ohio’s commitment to prevent double recovery does not cover

all relevant payments. If not corrected, this flawed commitment could be used to support

future double recovery or recovery of excessive rates from transmission customers that

did not cause the Network Upgrades at issue.

            Specifically, the sections of the CSA and the attached ESA referenced in footnote

19 relate only to the Customer’s responsibility to pay for exit fees (i.e., the Termination

filings committed to in AES Ohio’s Filing—such as revisions to Attachment H-15, rolled-in rate treatment
of the Network Upgrades, future phases of this data center, or other future large data center loads.

 Fee or Phase Termination Fee if the Customer cancels or decreases its expected energy

usage prior to taking service, or if it terminates service after energization but before the

end of the term of its ESA). 23 But AES Ohio’s commitment to prevent double recovery

(in footnote 19 of its transmittal letter) does not include the protections contained in

section 5.d of the ESA and section 3 of the CSA relating to Minimum Load charges and

deferral costs.

            Section 5.d of the ESA requires the Customer to make minimum payments if the

data center fails to operate at Minimum Load during the term of service. AES Ohio states

that this provision is “to protect AES Ohio, and its other customers, from having to incur

these substantial costs if Customer does not achieve commercial operations.” 24

Section 3(A) of the CSA provides that if AES Ohio stops work on a deferred phase of

construction at the request of the Customer, the Customer will pay a Deferral Payment

“consisting of a carrying charge applied to the plant constructed as of such deferral

date.” 25 AES Ohio states that the “Deferral Payment is intended to hold existing

customers and AES Ohio harmless for Customer’s decision to defer construction.” 26

            To ensure that the transmission cost of service reflects the results of the full set of

ratepayer protections provided for in the CSA and attached ESA, AES Ohio should

correct its commitment in footnote 19 to include the deferral costs and Minimum Load

Charges. To the extent AES Ohio does not make this important clarification on its own,

the Commission should require AES Ohio to do so or explain why Minimum Load

                                    CONCLUSION

       For the reasons stated above, the Commission should require AES Ohio to

(1) confirm that the “future AES Ohio rate case” proceeding on the rate treatment for the

facilities contemplated in the CSA will be filed pursuant to FPA section 205 in order to

ensure other transmission customers are not bearing the costs of Network Upgrades made

to serve data centers; and (2) include the Minimum Load charges and deferral costs

consistent with its commitment to protect against double recovery in footnote 19, or

explain why Minimum Load charges and deferral costs are excluded from this

commitment.
